I was not expecting it to be first on the list until very late in the day yesterday. I am here and prepared to proceed. I hope we can deal with this Bill now, as the Government says. Mr. Speaker, just to set the record straight on this matter, in the middle of this week I spoke with the Acting Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice. For many months the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) has not had a Parliamentary Secretary to work for him. We are still waiting for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to appoint one. Apparently there is some difficulty getting someone to work with the Minister.
Oh, oh!

I spoke in the middle of this week, to set the record very straight, with the Acting Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice. At that time I informed the Acting Parliamentary Secretary with respect to a technical amendment to Bill C-89 that we were certainly prepared to agree to it. We have supported this Bill in principle. We have worked to improve the legislation in the House and we will support the Bill at third reading.
Let us set the record straight in terms of the all-Party agreement. Yesterday I spoke again with the Acting Parliamentary Secretary. I spoke with the Government House Leader, and I indicated that we in the New Democratic Party were prepared to deal with this Bill early next week with very few speakers and to pass the legislation. In fact, I even suggested that perhaps in the middle of the week we might want to deal with the legislation at all stages, report stage and third reading, in one afternoon session. That was the agreement we made because we recognize the importance of the legislation.
Yesterday, immediately after the Question Period when the Government House Leader was asked what legislation would be before the House on Friday morning, he indicated that it would be the Western Diversification Act. Then he said that Bill C-74, the Environmental Protection Act would be called, followed by Bill C-92, amendments to the Wheat Board Act and Bill C-89, victims of crime. That was the order we were given yesterday afternoon at 3.15 p.m.
At approximately six o'clock yesterday afternoon we were phoned and told that all that was changed. The New Democratic Party House Leader, the Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap (Mr. Riis), was informed about six o'clock yesterday afternoon to forget what was said, that Bill C-89 was to come forward at 10 o'clock today. In other words, forget what he was told at 3.15. This House cannot function in that way. Some of us have responsibilities in our constituencies and we must have some notice.
The Acting Parliamentary Secretary is a man of honour, and he will know that the agreement very clearly was that this legislation would be dealt with next week and dealt with expeditiously. There was never any suggestion to the contrary. The Acting Parliamentary Secretary knows that.
When the Government attempts to change at the last minute the order of important legislation, despite indications of full co-operation from the Opposition, it still remains our responsibility to ensure that the legislation is given the kind of debate that is appropriate. A number of my caucus colleagues who want to speak on this legislation are unable to be here today. They assumed that the Government would act in good faith and would proceed as it indicated yesterday afternoon and as was indicated to me. Because of that, Mr. Speaker, we are given no alternative but to insist on a vote on this otherwise technical amendment and hope that the Government next time will co-operate with opposition critics in scheduling the debate for a time that is mutually agreeable.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words regarding this important interchange. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) indicated that he was quite prepared to debate this matter today. I feel sorry in a sense that he was given information that there had been some understanding because, as my hon. colleague, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) indicated, the Deputy House Leader said yesterday that today's business would be the Environmental Protection Act and we assumed that that was what the business would be. If we completed that legislation, we would then go on to the Wheat Board Act. Again, we assumed that that was what we would be doing later today. Consequently people made arrangements, assuming that what the Government said would be the business for Friday would be the business on Friday. But we found out late last night that there had been some changes.
In the meantime, I am afraid to say this but I say it with all sincerity to the Minister of Justice, the people who wanted to participate in the debate on this most important piece of legislation regarding victims of crime have left town for other business. I know the Minister knows that if people feel strongly about the issue they ought to have the opportunity to speak. I understand there was an agreement that we would be debating this matter presumably mid-week. As the Justice critic for the New Democratic Party has said, there was an indication that there would be a short list of speakers and that we would attempt to wrap up the matter in one day's debate. That is the way we do business, and I would like to think that is the way we will continue to do business.
We are trying, as Members of the New Democratic Party, to make the House of Commons work as effectively and as efficiently as possible. We are trying to conduct the business of the House of Commons in a business-like way, which means giving notice so that we can make plans and the debates can be informed and Members can participate in a positive way. We should deal with this legislation now. There is an amendment before the House. Let us deal with it and move on in an expeditious and positive way.

Western Economic Diversification Act WESTERN ECONOMIC DIVERSIFICATION ACT

The House resumed from Thursday, April 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mulroney that Bill C-113, an Act to promote the development and diversification of the economy of western Canada, to establish the Department of Western Economic Diversification and to make consequential amendments to other Acts, be read the third time and passed.
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure-
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I think the record will show that I was in mid-speech when we last handled this Bill, and I would like to complete my remarks.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Chair is very much in favour of an orderly proceeding this morning, and I am observing the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) who seems to be in agreement with the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), so I will recognize the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre on debate.

Mr. Speaker, when I was last interrupted, I was drawing to the attention of the House some of the difficulties I thought would arise as a result of the mandate for the western diversification office. I was commenting on the mandate, which is that the Western Diversification Office will represent the interests of western Canada in the development of national policies and the design of national programs and will ensure that western Canada is effectively linked to decision-making in Ottawa.
I had noted that the amount of federal moneys going to western Canada by way of federal expenditures for goods and services had actually dropped during the mandate of this Government. It had dropped from approximately 15 per cent to approximately 13 per cent. I was saying that it was indeed very necessary for someone in the Government to start looking after the interests of western Canada.
I find that this necessity is very hard to understand in light of the fact that throughout this Government's mandate, three of the four western provinces have been very supportive of the Government. Members of Parliament from government benches predominate in western Canada. In Alberta, for instance, there are no MPs except government MPs. Yet the amount of money going to the purchase of goods and services by the federal Government in western Canada declined. I can see why the Government felt it necessary to do something to increase the influence of westerners in the Government.
We all agree that the Senate is very ineffectual at representing regional interests and has never really performed that job, if in fact it was intended to perform that job in 1867 when the Constitution was put together. In spite of biannual and sometimes even more frequent meetings of the premiers, their

April 29, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
influence on the Government does not seem to be taking, even though most of them are supporters of the Government. The preponderance of MPs on the government side does not seem to be helping either.
Perhaps the problem then rests in the Cabinet. Does this Bill change that? I submit that it does not. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) will simply take on an extra responsibility. There will be no more votes in Cabinet and he will have no more power in Cabinet than he has now. How will western Canada be further represented and have its interests guarded, given that western Canada has already sent an overwhelming majority of government Members to Ottawa?
The Government's response has been to put another Deputy Minister outside Ottawa in Edmonton where he or she can speak on behalf of western Canada. Edmonton is a long way from Ottawa. The Premier of Alberta, when dealing with this Government, is finding that out. I do not understand how a Deputy Minister's voice will be any stronger with the Government than those of elected officials. I am concerned about whether or not the mandate of the Western Diversification Office will change the way western Canada is treated in confederation.
I would suspect that a Deputy Minister who is located in Ottawa might have more influence because of the way Ottawa Deputy Ministers function. There are meetings and official and unofficial gatherings. My understanding is that much of the interdepartmental work gets done at those kinds of functions. It will be difficult for a Deputy Minister located in Edmonton to exert the kind of influence that Deputy Ministers of other Departments influence over each other.
As I was pointing out the other day, there are some fairly strong Ministries with which the Western Diversification Office will have to deal. These Ministries also have an interest in western Canada as well as in other parts of the country and their final words tend to become law. The Ministry of Finance, for example, is now busily fighting inflation and the threat of inflation, even though in western Canada, the problem is deflation, not inflation. In my riding, property values have dropped by about 50 per cent since 1984. Yet the federal Government and the Department of Finance is fighting a war against inflation.
It is pretty hard to understand that we have inflation for those whose property values have dropped by 50 per cent, whether they own homes in small towns or farms in the agricultural area of my riding. For westerners, the focus on inflation does not seem to be a proper one. We are wondering who in Cabinet will be able to convince the Department of Finance of that fact.
In order to fight inflation, the Department of Finance has been raising interest rates. How does this help western Canada? Western Canadians are already carrying a very high debt load because of the depression. As incomes drop and property values drop, their ability to borrow money has
declined and interest rates are going back up. How will they be able to stay in business with interest rates rising?
Another factor that goes along with the business of raising interest rates is a policy of the Department of Finance which the Western Diversification Office and western MPs and cabinet Ministers will have to resist. It has raised the value of the Canadian dollar quite precipitously, more than 10 cents in the last year. What does that mean for my constituents and western Canadians? It means that the value of their wood products, their grain, and the oil that they export is down approximately 12 per cent in real value in terms of Canadian dollars from what it was one year ago. Not only are they having to fight a wrong-headed policy for their region, but they do not seem to be getting very much assistance from the premiers, from the Senators, or indeed from the government Members from that part of the country. The Western Diversification Office, and the creation of that office, will have great difficulty changing that, because so far all of the elements have appeared to be quite ineffectual in dealing with the interests of western Canada.

My colleague from the West referred especially to the problems of the agricultural economy, which have been devastating to western Canada. Since we have just had a national day of protest with respect to these agricultural problems, I would like to ask what his sense is of whether this Western Diversification Office is likely to provide any solutions or responses to those crises in agriculture, and what suggestions he might make as a counter to what the Conservatives have so far failed to do in western Canada?

One of the chief things that could be done to address the problem raised during the day of protest is to act on some of the proposals that have been put forward by the farm organizations, and the Senate agriculture committee, which published a report yesterday with regard to farm finance. In that report it pointed out that there were some 54,000 farmers across Canada who were in jeopardy of going out of business in the next year or two. This is close to 31 per cent of the active commercial farmers in the country. That committee report proposed a form of debt set aside, or a period of time when the farmers would not be required to pay interest on the debt that has accumulated over the past years. This would permit them to have a chance to get their feet under them, so to speak.
This proposal has the backing of most of the national farm organizations. It would have a great impact on maintaining the economy, especially the small economies in rural Canada, which rotate around small towns and villages. It would keep people on the farms and provide the population that is necessary to maintain the service sector in those small towns and villages.
The Government ought to be pursuing this approach more vigorously. It has had nearly four years to deal with this. It is
April 29, 1988

something that is known across the country as a $22 dilemma. The Canadian farming community owes $22 billion. This debt is far too high for the amount of income that can be generated from farm goods and services at the moment.

I wish to ask the Hon. Member a question, Mr. Speaker. The NDP was crying the blues when the Canadian dollar was devalued. Now the NDP is crying the blues when it is increasing in value. On which side of the issue did the NDP cry the loudest?

Any time that values change by 10 cents, which is the equivalent of 12 per cent or 13 per cent, in the course of one year, there is a very difficult readjustment to overcome. The rapidity of this adjustment will be felt in the export oriented community, which is basically the farmers of western Canada, and it will impact on them just as negatively as the rapid increase in the interest rates that we suffered under the Liberals. As the Hon. Member will recall, interest rates went from 12 per cent to 24 per cent in the course of approximately a year and a half. That virtually wiped out a lot of younger and growing farmers, farmers who had added to their debt load. This particular initiative that the Department of Finance is now engaged in will have exactly the same effect over the course of the next year or two, mark my words.

I would like my friend, the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre, to comment on whether the diversification fund will be put in a place where the funding will be equitably distributed among different regions and provinces in western Canada. When allocation of funding began, which I believe was prior to the legislation being adopted here, and there has already been some allocation take place, there was only what can appear like a politically motivated decision to make allocations and to talk about supporting different diversification projects in Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia, but not in Manitoba. In fact, the tap was very distinctly kept shut in Manitoba. I believe that that reflected political intervention by the present Government. It was attempting to make the New Democratic Party that was in power there look as though it could not deliver, because the diversification funds were not coming through. With the election in process, suddenly the tap opened up, because the Government was trying to show that somehow if the people voted Conservative, that would do good things.
It has not created a strong new government there. The new government is weak. In fact, it lost votes from the last election, where the Conservatives had more seats and more votes than they have now.
Does my hon. friend believe that this politically motivated interference will be acceptable to westerners, and will make the best use of taxpayers dollars, thus achieving the needed economic diversification in western Canada?

I think that the people of Manitoba showed that it was not acceptable. They gave Gary Filmon's Conservatives less seats than they had in the previous Government when
Western Economic Diversification Act
they were in opposition, and basically told the federal Government that they did not like the activities that the Conservative Party had engaged in in that province.
The reaction of westerners in general has been pretty much a wait-and-see attitude toward this initiative. Most westerners see it as a reshuffling of money and programs that did exist, and the hanging of a new sign on a lot of old programs. There has not been a lot of excitement one way or another. I note that the small business community has indicated that it is very fearful on the basis of some of the initial actions under the aegis of the Western Diversification Office, which appears to be more politically oriented than economically oriented. They have questioned some of the grants that have been made.
I remind the House that the initiatives are supposed to be targeted toward small and medium-sized businesses, yet one of the first diversification programs has been the announcement to assist a very large pulp and paper operation in northern Alberta. Another initiative was the creation of a national park, which is a very laudable use of federal money, but does not normally fall within the assistance of small and medium-sized businesses. It is small wonder that many westerners think that this will be used as much for a political slush fund as anything else.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on Bill C-113, an Act to promote the development and diversification of the economy of western Canada, to establish the Department of Western Economic Diversification and to make consequential amendments to other Acts. As other speakers have said, this Bill is a red herring to let the Government convince western Canadians that there is something new coming for that region of the country. Western Canadians are on to this scam and realize that this will not be the situation.
Government, of course, knows full well how regional development works and how it has worked for some time. We have had different programs. We have had regional bodies and regional programs. We had the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and then the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. As we go along it seems that the commitment of the early 1970s to regional development is not getting stronger but weaker. The Government does not have the conviction to proceed with regional development.
The four western provinces and the four Atlantic provinces seem to be forgotten more and more with each passing year as far as this very important principle is concerned. That is evident. If we look at the facts and look deeply into the structure of how the Government has disbursed funds, we will see that this is very evident. This evidence is apparent in the closing of rail lines, the reduction of postal services, and the general reduction of government services which are important if people are going to locate business enterprises in western Canada. This cannot continue to be the case. If we continue

April 29, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
the present trend of centralization, Canada as we know it will disappear.
In Canada we have approximately 800 one-industry towns. That is why we have been trying to convince the Minister of Finance to continue with flow-through shares as a means of continuing real, meaningful regional development. If we do away with flow-through shares we will hurt the mining industry, which is a large support for those 800 one-industry towns. It is the one industry in many of the towns as is the fishing industry in many other towns. Flow-through shares are a very important part of regional development, yet they are not mentioned in this Bill.
On March 4, 1987, the federal Government announced the amalgamation of the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion and the Ministry of Science and Technology to form the Department of Industry, Science and Technology. The responsibility for regional development functions was given to ACOA in Atlantic Canada, to the Northern Ontario Advisory Board for northern Ontario, and to the Department of Western Economic Diversification for western Canada, the head office to be located in Edmonton, Alberta.
This is another reorganization, it is a shuffling of the cards and no more. Each time the cards are shuffled something falls from the table, something very important for regional development, something from the fibre of this very important process. When we went from DREE to DRIE we lost a lot of commitment from the Government on regional development. We are again losing a great deal.
The new Department of Industry, Science and Technology will deal with a number of things which will be mainly in central Canada. The Government has parcelled out a sum of money to northern Ontario, to Atlantic Canada, and to western Canada. It said "Here is your fund, don't bother us any more. This is what you are going to get, now be quiet".
In addition to co-ordinating federal programs in western Canada, this Western Diversification Fund, which will be $1.2 billion over five years, is going to be insufficient to meet the economic needs in western Canada. As my colleagues from Winnipeg-Fort Garry and Algoma have noted, this $1.2 billion over five years amounts to $220 million a year, which will not be sufficient to meet the purposes which the Government would like us to believe it intends for western Canada.
By 1983-84 a commitment for $1.2 billion was made to western Canada under the ERDA agreement. This was matched by the provincial governments for a total of $2.1 billion. It is obvious that the Western Diversification Fund is not generous and that it is not a new initiative by the Government. The question is what moneys which are presently in the system are going to be taken from other programs and put into the Western Diversification Fund. How much of this is new money?
The Government also wants us to believe that this system of regional development through a department or agency in a
particular region is going to be easier for people in Atlantic Canada, northern Ontario, and western Canada. The Government has told us that this money will be looked after by people from the region and will be more sympathetically allotted throughout the respective areas. That would be fine if that were what the Government really intended.
The recommendations and studies done by the Government on how to approach regional development specified that if you are going to have a regional agency, it must be non-political. You cannot put people in control who have political backgrounds or are in any way identified with political operations.
The Government has not followed this recommendation. It succumbed to the temptation of putting in people who have been connected with the Progressive Conservative Party. That is bad because, even if the Government did not intend it, as happens in many cases where there are political appointments, the first thing to be looked after is the political connections. That does not always mean that the best projects are funded. It means that the best political contacts are funded.
This is a travesty. We are telling the people of western Canada, Atlantic Canada, and northern Ontario that this is going to be something new, that the frustrations with regional development over the years are going to be met, that things are different now. However, things are not going to be different. Things cannot be different until the Government develops a purposeful will to get out of the political business in dealing with the welfare of the regions of the country.
I see that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) is in the House today. On March 29 I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) a question on the Canadian Exploration Development Incentive Program of which the Minister is well aware. The Minister of Energy and the rest of the Government are planning to reduce CEDIP considerably by October 1 of this year. At present CEDIP refunds one-third of investments of up to $10 million by particular companies in the oil and gas industry.
This was wonderful for small companies. While it may not have been the best program that could have been developed, it was an initiative taken by the Government. It was a step in the right direction that was much appreciated by small oil and gas companies in western Canada. This fund was introduced when oil prices were low in an attempt to help small companies that are so very important to the oil and gas industry in western Canada. They have come to depend on this funding, much of which is spent on exploration and development.
When oil prices rose, the Government felt that it could reduce these funds. Rather than a one-third refund it is considering a one-sixth refund, to take effect October 1. There is a significant difference between one-third of $10 million and one-sixth of $10 million, and our Party and small producers have suggested to the Government that rather than making a change by reducing the 33.3 per cent refund to 16 2/3 per cent,
April 29, 1988

it should reduce the $10 million to $5 million. It would still protect the smaller companies and give the full percentage they have at the present time.
The Government has not responded to this suggestion, and refuses to make a commitment. I believe the Government is letting down the small oil and gas producers in this country. There is no need for a royal commission or an investigation in this particular area. The Government only needs to make a decision, but that is not forthcoming.
Let us consider the free trade agreement. It may seem to the energy sector that it will be able to sell more oil and gas into the United States, but it is not taking into consideration the ramifications of the omnibus trade Bill. If that passes, it will be a severe deterrent to our trading rights with the United States.
Last spring the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) spoke to the people in Alberta and said that the regulations imposed by the U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission on the sale of natural gas through the pipeline system into the United States was wrong. He said that it was extraterritorial and that the United States had no right to do this. However, when the free trade agreement was negotiated, the National Energy Board was almost completely decimated. Its powers have been severely reduced so that even if it is able to function, we do not know if it will have any meaningful effect.
In return, the United States was required to do very little. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission was left almost completely intact. The agreement contains only a nebulous comment which states that the federal Government of Canada and the United States Government will enter into negotiations to try to work at reducing the regulatory network that exists in the two countries. That is not good enough. The Prime Minister told the people in western Canada that this arrangement would not be good enough, but the changes he was seeking did not occur. One must ask if the Government has any real intention to strengthen regional development in western Canada.
We have to consider the CF-18 contract and other contracts for which western Canada had every right to be considered but was ignored. We have not seen any real change in the Government's lack of commitment to western Canada.
The Government must do more than simply offer $120 million and ask to be left alone. It must have a comprehensive plan to meet the aspirations of western Canada. It must introduce such a plan soon in order to address the difficulties facing the West, with lower prices and fewer problems in the agricultural industry. The Government is only paying lip service to farmers at a time when families in western Canada who have been in farming for generations are losing their farms. Yet the Government continues on in the belief that western Canada will accept a pittance in the form of a slush fund and forget that western Canada will be ignored as a vital centre of this country, which it should really be.

subsubtopic: SUPREME COURT DECISION-CALL FOR GOVERNMENT ACTION OF FETAL RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the recent Supreme Court ruling on abortion, all seven Justices said that they were not deciding on the rights of the fetus but that there is a valid state objective to do so. They also made it clear that the state interest in protecting the fetus increases as it develops.
The bedrock of fundamental justice cannot be based on arbitrary gestation periods. If life gains value as it matures, does it lose value as it gets much older? I think not.
Dr. Albert Schweitzer said: "If a man loses reverence for any part of life, he will lose reverence for all life".
The Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops wrote recently: "For us to accept abortion would be to deny our belief in the value of human life".
I urge our Government to act quickly on fetal rights, to develop comprehensive national programs that show abortion is no answer to unwanted pregnancies, to strengthen services to help pregnant women and unwanted children, and to do what is morally right and not allow abortion on demand.

Mr. Speaker, the acid rain saga with the United States continued yesterday when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that a treaty on acid rain between Canada and the United States is inevitable, just as surely as summer follows spring.
Apparently the President will ask George Shultz to discuss Canada's eight-point proposal for an acid rain accord as a matter of priority with our External Affairs Minister. But in his remarks the Prime Minister did not mention that in January this year such a plan was examined by the United States and rejected by the same George Shultz. In addition, Michael Perley of the Canadian Coalition on Acid Rain scoffed at the Prime Minister's assertion that shifting the issue to Shultz is a sign of progress. He said:

April 29, 1988
This is just a repetition of what has already been done. It is a sign that the Prime Minister failed to get the President to act. Reagan never had any intention of doing anything on acid rain.
Unfortunately, we seem to be back to square one.

Mr. Speaker, in the April 28 edition of The Globe and Mail, Brian Milner writes as follows:
Manitoba's new Government is stepping into a financial quagmire with little room to manoeuvre ...
That is the harsh assessment of Dominion Bond Rating Service .. . which paints a picture of persistent economic mismanagement by former Premier Howard Pawley's New Democrats.
The lessen is clear. An NDP Government means economic stagnation and social regression. Barret destroyed the British Columbia economy. Pawley did likewise in Manitoba. We must never, ever, let Broadbent and his gang similarly ruin Canada.

Mr. Speaker, farmers and small businessmen in Canada know the economic devastation that was created when the Bank of Canada, under a Liberal Government, permitted interest rates to rise from 12 per cent to 24 per cent in a very short period of time. They could not adjust their price. They could only suffer and incur debt. This Government is also adding an equally devastating debt burden to farmers and small business people who export their products. By raising the Canadian dollar, it is reducing the export value of these products, again forcing these people into debt.
Farmers do not need more debt. It is inappropriate at a time when the Senate Agriculture Committee report of yesterday estimates that 31 per cent of Canada's farmers are practically insolvent due to debt. It calls for a relief scheme where the Government would pay all or part of a farmer's interest charges for a fixed period, for a restructuring of debt on more favourable terms, and extensions of repayment periods. It also calls for the establishment of a secondary loan market similar to CMHC.
The Government has used up nearly four years of its mandate. When will it address the problem, the $22 billion problem?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to remind Hon. Members and the general public that this week is National Organ Donor Awareness Week. Our Government, through our Minister of National Health and Welfare, works with various agencies to help inform the public and health professionals of the benefits of transplants and the need for organ and tissue donors.
I invite all Canadians to take a moment to think about becoming donors and discuss their decisions with members of their families. Through organ donations, each one of us can give the most generous gift there is, the gift of life.
However, Mr. Speaker, my invitation specifically excludes all Members of the PD Caucus. That tribe should not be allowed to reproduce in any way whatsoever!

Mr. Speaker, all Canadians are equal before the law. The Devine government in Saskatchewan is now violating this fundamental principle of a democracy by abolishing the Fransaskois' basic rights and replacing them with a misleading law that gives the government absolute discretionary power.
This kind of action by Saskatchewan threatens the future of all linguistic minorities in the country, be they English- or French-speaking. We do not want any politician to be able to play with the basic rights of minorities, which are already too fragile and vulnerable.
Respect for minorities is an essential feature of Canada, one which makes our country a distinct society. Minorities do not need fine speeches. They need results in order to live fully.
Bill 2 violates the spirit of Canadian society. It is mean-spirited because it rejects existing rights instead of guaranteeing them and then finding ways to implement them appropriately.
It is regrettable that the Government did not see fit to consult the Fransaskois because their demands are reasonable and their future is at stake. I believe that the Conservative Government has not played a constructive, helpful role in this affair.
April 29, 1988

Mr. Speaker, 40 years ago 70 per cent of the Canadian workforce was engaged in the resource and manufacturing industries. Today in 1988 industries using new-wrought information technology employ an ever increasing number of persons. Within the Canadian economy, total revenue for knowledge intensive industries in 1987 was $18 billion and those industries employed more than 230,000 persons.
The information technology sector is growing quickly. The knowledge intensive sector is expected to grow at an annual rate of 15.5 per cent, much faster than the Gross Domestic Product. The software and services segment of this industry is growing at an annual rate of 20 per cent. Information technology spending has accounted for 35 per cent of all R and D initiatives in Canada in recent years.
Canada's standard of living ultimately depends on its success in exporting internationally competitive goods and services, but our advantages in the natural resource industries are being severely challenged by other nations. Our future lies in exporting information technology. As the natural resource industries lose ground, knowledge intensive industries will provide opportunities for Canada to seize world export markets and bolster our standard of living.

subtopic: NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY AMENDMENTS TO LEGISLATION
NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY AMENDMENTS TO LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Conservative majority of this House voted against a series of amendments made by the New Democratic Party to improve the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. These amendments would focus the agency on attacking regional disparity, guarantee fairness between the Atlantic provinces, and ensure that the ACOA board would be representative of all interests in economic development, not just a narrow view.
The Government refused to support these amendments and went further in this week's debate by having members of Cabinet, including the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), attack members of this Party for speaking out for Atlantic Canada on the grounds that they represent Ontario ridings.
With this attitude of the Government it is no wonder that Atlantic Canada is not treated fairly. New Democratic Members of Parliament from all over Canada will continue to fight for regional development in Atlantic Canada in spite of government opposition. This fight will continue until regional
disparity is eliminated and Atlantic Canadians are treated fairly and have equal opportunities with the rest of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, 1 want to emphasize the seriousness of the phase out of flowthrough shares. The White Paper of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) issued in June, 1987, does change the value and use of flow-through shares. This vehicle has been used by small and medium-sized resource companies, oil, gas, and mining, to raise capital for exploration and development, especially in our remote areas. It has created hundreds of thousands of jobs all across Canada.
To explore is a high-risk business. Flow-through is probably the only way for juniors to raise cash in a high-risk industry. I urge the Government to review this severe situation immediately.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):

We are not talking about cutting a ribbon or cracking a bottle of champagne. We are talking about breaking the bottleneck that prevents economic growth and activity, and jobs in a region with unemployment of 30 per cent, from going ahead.

April 29, 1988
For God's sake, let's get the ball rolling. Let's make the harbour development happen. Let's let economic activity move ahead in Humber-Port au Port Ste. Barbe and, in particular, in the city of Corner Brook and let's do it now.

subtopic: ACID RAIN-PRIME MINISTER'S ADDRESS TO UNITED STATES CONGRESS
ACID RAIN-PRIME MINISTER'S ADDRESS TO UNITED STATES CONGRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) speech to the U.S. Congress was a great success. It drew the attention of the American public to the very serious problem of acid rain. It was educational in that many people who live outside the northeastern states in America had no knowledge of the seriousness of the problem of acid rain.
It is clear from the response of callers to an open line call-in show on an American network that people in all parts of the U.S. are now taking notice. Americans have been calling their Congressmen to let them know that they want something done.
It has taken a number of years to educate Canadians about the devastating effects of acid rain. The awareness and education process of Americans was certainly enhanced by the Prime Minister's address to Congress. The general public in the U.S. is beginning to take notice of this serious problem. For that we must thank our Prime Minister and our Government for giving this issue the importance it deserves by raising it not only in the minds of elected representatives in the United States but also with the American public.

subtopic: ENTRENCHMENT OF FRENCH LANGUAGE RIGHTS IN THE YUKON
ENTRENCHMENT OF FRENCH LANGUAGE RIGHTS IN THE YUKON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this week marked a historic step in the constitutional development of the Yukon when an agreement was signed between the Yukon Territorial Government and the federal Government to entrench French language rights in the territorial Legislature and courts.
In recognition as well of the cultural and historical importance of aboriginal languages in the territory, an agreement was also made regarding a start on developing essential services in the seven aboriginal languages as well.
This is an important step forward in the Yukon. It recognizes the contribution of Francophone people within the Yukon and their rights, and also the important language and cultural development of aboriginal people, the Yukon's first citizens.

CONTRIBUTION BY FORESTERS TO NATIONAL ECONOMY

The contribution of our foresters to our national economy is truly something to celebrate.

subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the subject of acid rain, we had the Prime Minister's admission of failure on television last evening, when he said: "Well, what do you do? What do you do with the United States? Do you declare war?"
We would not ask for that, but we do want the Prime Minister to declare war on acid rain, and to tell the President of the United States that this is the single most important bilateral issue between our two countries at the moment.
My question of the Prime Minister is this. Why did he not tell the President and the U.S. Congress that the situation in respect of acid rain is of crucial and vital importance to Canada; that our priority is not a technological deal on nuclear submarines, but to clean up the environment of our two countries?
The Prime Minister knows as well as I do that the U.S. generates six million tonnes of acid rain-causing emissions every year, and that those emissions are killing our rivers and lakes.
Why does the Prime Minister not admit to the country that he has failed to persuade the President and the Congress on this very vital issue to Canadians?

The House resumed debate on the motion of Mr. Mulroney that Bill C-113, an Act to promote the development and diversification of the economy of western Canada, to establish the Department of Western Economic Diversification and to make consequential amendments to other Acts, be read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, several times in the past we in the West have heard about western diversification. As far back as 1911, 1912, 1913 the hue and cry was to diversify. We moved into massive irrigation projects. The Bassano dam was built, and irrigation projects were undertaken east of Calgary and between Calgary and Medicine Hat. A few years later irrigation projects were undertaken in the Lethbridge area. All of that was in aid of diversification.
During the war, western agriculture diversified into a variety of vegetable crops, including sugar beets. In the late 1950s, early 1960s, we were again advised to diversify. The hue and cry went out from the four provincial Governments and the federal Government that we had to attract more industry, and we did. From the late 1940s on, we had tremendous development in oil wells, gas wells, potash mines, and so forth.
In 1968-69, we again heard the cry that we had to diversify. Grain prices had gone all to heck. We were up to our ears in grain, literally speaking. Farmers diversified into livestock, establishing hog operations, cow-calf operations, and beef cattle operations. We had feedlots by the dozens, all over the West, to the point where we were shipping too many to the United States, resulting in the U.S. imposing a countervail and imposing quotas on product going from western Canada into U.S. markets. As well, at that time the Canadian dollar was trading at par with its U.S. counterpart. As a result, feedlots all over the West were going bankrupt. To give some indication of how depressed grain prices were in 1968-69, one could buy three bushels of barley for $1. So much for that diversification effort. That was the third or fourth diversification effort to go down the drain.
I heard the Hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) say earlier today that the NDP had been crying about the dollar going down, and now we were crying about it going up.
I have never heard any Member of my Party cry about the dollar going down. I wish it would go down much lower. I wish it would get down to 65 or 70 cents vis-a-vis the U.S. dollar. It is when the Canadian dollar is at that level vis-a-vis the U.S. dollar that we do well with exports. As well, Canadian manufactured and processed products can better compete in
April 29, 1988

the domestic market in competition with imports from the U.S. and other parts of the world.
If the Government of Canada manipulates the Canadian dollar to higher levels vis-a-vis the U.S. dollar, the producers, processors and manufacturers in the Atlantic provinces and the western provinces are going to have that much more difficulty, not only in competing in the markets in central Canada, but in U.S. markets, or markets anywhere else in the world.
Unless some fundamental change is made in policy direction, no diversification plan in the world will work. While there may be some salutary effects for a few hundred small businesses-and that is something about which I would not complain-the basic problem would remain.
The objective of this measure is to bring about increased diversification in western Canada and in Atlantic Canada, with a move to larger and more efficient modes of production, processing and manufacturing. No one can be against that. Who would not be in favour of that? However, since Atlantic Canada and western Canada have small markets, the problem then is how we get the products to the large market, in competition with those who produce, process or manufacture the same or similar products in central Canada or central and eastern United States. We have to compete.
We are quite happy to compete on quality, quantity, warranties and reliability. We can do those things in western Canada and Atlantic Canada as well as those in any place else in the whole continent. However, we also must compete against geography, against interest rates and against a Canadian dollar that is rising in comparison to the American dollar. Those are three major handicaps, and we have found out in the past that those handicaps have caused diversification ideas, as good as they were, to fail.
It seems to me that there must be a fundamental national policy of discrimination, not discrimination against the large industrial and manufacturing complexes from Quebec City to Windsor, but discrimination in favour of the western provinces, Atlantic Canada, northern Ontario and northern Quebec. One of the ways to do that is to do something about transportation costs.
In my province, there is a first-class poultry operation. It is located at Wynyard, Saskatchewan, 200 miles from Regina. The grocery stores in my city sell those chickens. However, over the last several months, we have found that there are chickens from elsewhere for sale in that store as well. Those chickens are from Georgia, 2,000 miles away, while Wynyard is 200 miles away.
Those chickens from Georgia are good chickens. There is no problem with their quality. The Wynyard operator also has an excellent operation. He has received grants and loans from the provincial and federal Governments. He employs a few dozen people. It is a family-owned and operated business and he pays
Western Economic Diversification Act
a good wage. In Georgia, they pay $1.65 per hour. I do not think there is one single self-respecting businessman in all of Canada who would lower himself to paying that kind of a wage. That is why the poultry producer in Georgia can place chickens in the Regina market for just as cheap as our own operator in Wynyard, 200 miles away. That is one of the handicaps we face in western Canada and in Atlantic Canada. Therefore, we need transportation assistance.
The programs that presently exist must be improved, and as well, we need additional programs. If the national Government really wants to do something about western diversification, let me suggest that we return to what we were doing up until 1960 when anywhere from five to 20 trainloads of coal moved out of Saskatchewan, Alberta and eastern British Columbia per day, destined for Ontario. That was low-sulphur coal that did not cause acid rain. Since that time, there have been no trainloads of coal moving from western Canada to the Ontario hydro plants. Those plants are burning high-sulphur coal from Virginia and Kentucky.
When we were debating the abolishment of the Crow rate in the House in 1982 and 1983, one of the things we said then, and we say again now, is that we need not only a Crow rate for grain but a Crow rate for coal and a Crow rate for a whole host of other products so that the transportation costs of a manufacturing plant in Alberta can be equalized with those of a manufacturing plant in southern Ontario. Then these plants would have to compete only on the quality of their products, their reliability, their serviceability and their warranties. They would have to compete in areas where the real competition should exist. Unless those who start industries in western Canada and Atlantic Canada can get their products to market at a cost no greater than their competitors in Boston, New York, Toronto or Montreal, they do not have a prayer.
There is another little item that could be helpful. This Government has made much of the whole issue of western diversification. One would have thought that in four years this Government would have made a calculated and deliberate move to increase the purchases made by the national Government in western Canada and Atlantic Canada and decrease the purchases made in Ontario and Quebec. That would be an example of discriminating in favour of the West and the Atlantic provinces.
What has happened instead? In 1984-85, this Government purchased 13.9 per cent of its requirements through Supply and Services in western Canada. In 1985-86, that figure went down to 12.8 per cent. In 1986-87, it went down further to 11.5 per cent.
We are not talking about peanuts here. The total figure for purchases in the four western provinces plus the Yukon and the Northwest Territories in 1986-87 was over $900 million, and that is only 11.8 per cent of the federal Government's purchases. Quebec got 32 per cent and there is a smaller population in Quebec than there is in the four western

Western Economic Diversification Act
provinces. Ontario, with a slightly higher population than the four western provinces, got 44 per cent.
In the Atlantic provinces, the picture is even worse. Federal government purchases from the four Atlantic provinces amounted to 7 per cent of the total. I suppose the Atlantic provinces would have something in the order of 3.5 million to 4 million people. They received 7 per cent, which was down from what they spot in the Atlantic provinces in 1985-86.
I have mentioned two areas where if we want to do something about diversification and greater opportunity for farmers, businessmen, and fishermen, we would redirect a lot of the government purchases that are required. Some of it could be diverted from offshore purposes without jeopardizing some of the purchases made in central Canada. We purchased billions from other parts of the world and from the United States.
I mentioned the whole matter of coal. There is at least a 500-year supply of low sulphur coal in western Canada. There is not a single mine left operating in the whole Drumheller Valley. There may be one left operating in the Crow's Nest Pass. The only reason there are strip mines in southern Saskatchewan is because the coal is being used by Saskatchewan Power Corporation, otherwise we would not be moving any of it. Here is an area of massive development-
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I would like to call a quorum.
I see a quorum. The debate will continue.

I thank my colleague for doing that. I want my good friends opposite to be able to enjoy my remarks.
I want to mention the main items that would ensure the success of diversification and opportunity for Atlantic Canada and for western Canada; have the Canadian dollar go down, reduce interest rates and, if necessary, bring in limited foreign exchange. If an investor in Canada wants to invest in some processing or manufacturing, and he wants to do it in the United States, he could be given a tax incentive to do it in Canada and it will cost him if he tries to do it somewhere else.
We must also look at Canadian history and remember and realize that transportation subsidies of various types, direct and indirect, are an absolute necessity for western Canada and for Atlantic Canada to be able to diversify their economies and compete where the markets are in central Canada and the heavily populated areas of the United States. Without that, no matter what political Party is in power, efforts to diversify the economies of northern Ontario, and northern Quebec, Atlantic and western Canada are doomed to failure. It has been tried before without ensuring that the things I have mentioned were in place. I hope that the Government's program for western development succeeds, but I am warning that it cannot succeed
unless interest rates are reduced, unless the value of the Canadian dollar in relation to the United States dollar goes down, and unless something more is done about subsidizing transportation costs for our processors and manufacturers in those other regions of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to participate in the debate regarding western Canada. As a western Canadian I must say that I remember when there were thousands of small and medium sized businesses in western Canada requesting assistance of one type or another from the federal Government to allow them to expand into new product lines and new markets, and we kept hearing that there was not any money available. Then the announcement was made that the Ghermezian brothers received $5 million from the federal Government for Fantasy-land. They are one of the richest families in Canada, they have one of the largest and most powerful industrial business conglomerates in Canada; and they received $5 million from the federal Government.
We remember that because it seemed to send a certain signal that, if you were a small western business person or a struggling westerner trying to establish a business or to expand a business, there were no funds available. However, if you had political connections with the Conservative Party, and presumably had lots of campaign funds, you could ask for $5 million and would receive it. Many westerners remember that day.
They also remember the day regarding the CF-18 maintenance contract where virtually every adviser to the federal Government said that the maintenance contract for the CF-18 fighter planes should be given to Bristol Aerospace in Winnipeg; in other words, a western Canadian maintenance operator. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) overruled every adviser and said that that maintenance contract would go to Quebec.
That was a political decision, and the Prime Minister has the right to make political decisions. However, he should have had the gumption and the intestinal fortitude to stand up and say: "I am going to make a political decision which goes against all the advice that I have received, which goes against sound business reasoning, which goes against running a decent, up-front Government, and I am making this political decision". He did not, Mr. Speaker. He fumbled and fiddled around for days attempting to justify how he knew better than all of the advisers regarding the maintenance contract for the CF-18s. Of course, western Canada lost that contract.
We also remember that not long ago Preston Manning decided that he needed to found a new political Party in the West because the Conservatives had let westerners down. They had sent a lot of Conservatives to Parliament to reverse the dastardly deeds that Liberals had been doing to western Canadians for so many years. What is the record, Mr. Speaker? When he formed the Reform Party, a western
April 29, 1988

Canadian Party, Preston Manning stated that the situation has actually worsened under the Mulroney Government.
Then a few weeks ago the Premier from British Columbia indicated that he had had enough; British Columbians were fed up with always getting the short end of the stick, always getting short shrift, being left out of federal government programs, and never getting their fair share. The Premier went on to explain that British Columbia represents a major portion of the Canadian population. It pays in excess of $11 billion annually to the federal coffers in terms of corporate and personal income tax. The number of federal government contracts and supply and service contracts were almost infinitesimal.
Earlier this week people representing the printing industry in British Columbia came to lobby. They stated that although British Columbia has almost 11 per cent of the population, it received less than 1 per cent of all of the federal government printing contracts. In other words, the lion's share of printing federal government brochures and of all printing that the federal Government does goes to central Canadian printers. The representatives of the printers stated that they wanted to get their fair share, and 1 per cent is not a fair share to British Columbia.
I could go on and on about others from western Canada who have registered their disappointment and disillusionment of the West not receiving its fair share.
The federal Government then decided to set up the western development office with a western development fund of $1.2 billion over five years, which comes to about $60 million per province per year. This was going to be the major government initiative to diversify the western economy.
The first announcement made was that the money required to develop South Moresby Park, $79 million, would be coming from the Western Diversification Fund rather than the Policy Revenue Fund from where money normally comes to develop a national park. A few days later another announcement was made. The funding for the Salmonid Enhancement Program for British Columbia, $53.7 million, would not come from the fisheries budget, from where one would normally expect it to come, but from the Western Diversification Fund as well. That is British Columbia taken care of for two or three years. It is like a shell game-now you see it, now you don't.
I decided that it was time to do a little research to find out what the situation was. I listened to one of the cabinet Ministers, the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer) from Manitoba, who said with regard to the Western Development Fund:
It sounds like a lot of money, but in the over-all scheme of things it is not
that great.
That was a Minister of the Crown saying that the amount of funds is not that great.
Western Economic Diversification Act
I noticed that the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) spoke to the Rotary Club just after the announcement was made and was quoted in the Edmonton Journal as saying:
The recently announced western diversification strategy,... is certainly a
modest step in the right direction-but certainly inadequate in its funding.
One of the most outspoken western Members of Parliament has said that it is inadequate.
Two days after the announcement The Financial Post said that there is no doubt whatever the potential contribution of Ottawa's western diversification initiative is truly piddling. The Financial Post called the amount of money piddling in terms of western diversification.
One of the senior officers of the Western Diversification Office, whose name I will not mention because it would not be fair to him, said on the public record that the fund is not all that big when you look at the amount of capital.
I could go on with a whole list of people who are members of the Cabinet, members of the Government, or senior officials in economic development portfolios for the federal Government, saying that this is an inadequate amount of funds to do anything. However, that is a little too close to the Government.
Let us go to one of the spokespersons for small and mediumsized business in Canada. Mr. John Bulloch heads up the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. He put out a report from which I will read only two or three things, because that is all I have time for. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business said that the Western Development Fund "is a political slush fund to support vulnerable constituencies".
The Canadian Federation of Independent Business calls it a political slush fund. Good for John Bulloch for having the courage to speak out and call it what it is. He went on to say that it is also a "bureaucratic slush fund available for other line Departments of the Ministers to raid in lieu of other national programs that should have their fair share spent in the West". It is a slush fund for the politicians and for the bureaucrats.
He went on to say that it is a "narrow and highly concentrated centralized approach to diversification".
There is no grass roots involvement; it does not involve the people. A few bureaucrats headquartered in Edmonton will be making the decisions on western diversification based on political slush.
Mr. Bulloch went on to say that the Western Diversification Office was "a confusing black box lacking clear criteria or policy direction, and on a collision course with a myriad of client groups who are inevitably going to see thousands of applications rejected and thousands of hopes dashed".
I hate to say it, Mr. Speaker, but that is what has happened. In my own constituency there is a group called the Thompson

April 29, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
Nicola Manufacturers Association representing 500 manufacturing enterprises in the Kamloops region. They are struggling to co-ordinate organizations and represent manufacturers wanting to expand their operations. They went to the Western Diversification Fund and requested a paltry $40,000 per year for the next two years. They said that within two years their income from marketing royalties and software sales would be sufficient to ensure their ongoing financial independence.
Did the Western Diversification Fund support the Thompson Nicola Manufacturers Association to diversify the economy of central British Columbia to the tune of $40,000 a year for two years? No. It was rejected. I guess we should be asking the Ghermezian brothers to apply for us because they obviously have the right connections. They can get $5 million to build Fantasyland in Edmonton, but we cannot get $40,000 to expand a manufacturing base in western Canada.
Let us go on. Let us look at the facts. We have heard a lot of rhetoric and a lot of flim-flam and shell games. Let us look at the facts with regard to industrial assistance between September, 1984, and March, 1986, the last period for which we have good data. Over that period of time British Columbia received $47 million, Saskatchewan received $18 million, Alberta received $16 million, and Manitoba received $13 million, for a total of $111 million. In the same time frame Ontario received $260 million and Quebec received $430 million.
Once again the West did not get its fair share. We are not saying that Quebec should not get that amount of money or that Ontario should not get that kind of industrial assistance support. However, we are saying that the West should get its fair share; nothing more, just its fair share. However, it is not getting its fair share.
Let us refer back to the report which the Canadian Federation of Independent Business put together for parliamentarians. They talked about procurement, the fancy word for the federal Government buying things from western Canada. They said that with 11.4 per cent of the population, British Columbia received only 3.6 per cent of federal government procurement. Alberta won only 3.6 per cent of the contract even though it has 9.3 per cent of the Canadian population. Saskatchewan has 4 per cent of the population and gets only 1 per cent of government contracts, and Manitoba has 4.2 per cent of the population of Canada and gets only 2.8 per cent of the contracts. However, Ontario and Quebec together receive 76 per cent of all government contracts.
The source of this is not a partisan research division. It is the Canadian Federation of Independent Business in a report dated April 12, 1988, which points out that government supply and service comes overwhelmingly from central Canada.
Let us go on and look at Employment and Immigration. The Estimates indicate that last year the Department of Employment and Immigration spent $479 million in the West. Next year Employment and Immigration will spend $339 million in the West. That is a net reduction of nearly $140 million. At a time when the West is struggling to play its rightful role in the
Canadian economy, rather than providing support or even maintaining support the federal Government is cutting back on employment funds for western Canada.
Let us look, for example, at all supply and service purchases from western Canada. In the early 1960s, before the present Government took office, the federal Government purchased about 16 per cent of all its supplies from western Canada. When the Government of the present Prime Minister was elected in 1984 that had fallen to 13.9 per cent. In 1985 that had fallen to 12.8 per cent, and in the past year it fell to 11.5 per cent. There are the facts in black and white. Under this Conservative Government procurement in western Canada has actually decreased every year.
The West has 28 per cent of the population, and when we are told that the Government only purchases 11.5 per cent of its supplies from western Canada we get angry and upset. That is why western Canadians are telling the Government that we have had enough.
Let us go on. I have piles of material here which indicate that in virtually every Department the West is getting shafted, the West is getting the short shrift, the West is getting the short end of the stick.
With regard to service contracts I will compare, for example, Ontario and British Columbia. British Columbia is representative of any of the four western provinces. The information indicates that in 1986-87, the most recent year for which we have data, Ontario received $206 million in service contracts and British Columbia received $21 million in service contracts. When you consider the population of Ontario and British Columbia, you realize that there is no way British Columbia should get such an infinitesimal amount of contracts in terms of money.
Ontario received $138 million worth of goods and services contracts while B.C. received $15 million in contracts. When one adds up all the different contracts, including industrial cooperation, equipment contracts, goods contracts and service contracts, Ontario received $360 million worth in the last year while B.C. received $41 million. This is more evidence to indicate that British Columbia, like all western provinces, has to receive what it ought to receive in terms of federal Government investment in developing economic infrastructure.
I have already talked about the CF-18 contract. I have not mentioned the gas taxes that keep rising by one, two, or three cents a litre. It is westerners who are hurt the most by an increase in transportation cost. Westerners must travel over vast distances not only in terms of moving goods but for personal transportation.

What about interest rate policy? The Governor of the Bank of Canada says that high interest rates are required to dampen the fires of inflation in Ontario. What about the

West? There are no fires of inflation in the West. Inflation is extremely low in the West, because many areas still face severe economic depression. The interest rate policy of the Government discriminates against western Canadian enterprises and western Canadian consumers.
Let us consider flow-through shares. 1 give credit to an Hon. Member from Calgary who earlier today stood in her place, as others have, to say that the Government must change its attitude about flow-through shares.
The flow-through share mechanism allowed small and medium sized resource companies in Canada, particularly in western Canada, to obtain the necessary capital to expand and explore for more deposits. It created tens of thousands of jobs in the most remote areas of Canada.
However, it did not create many jobs in downtown Toronto or in the heart of the cities. The Government proceeded to gut this program that was assisting western Canada. The prospectors, placer miners, the smaller junior mining companies and oil companies are on bended knee asking for a chance in western Canada. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) simply tells them that the Government has decided to do away with this program that provides so many benefits to junior oil and mining companies in western Canada.
It came to my attention recently that while there will be the Western Diversification Fund in western Canada, and a new agency in Atlantic Canada, the new Department of Industry, Science and Technology retains the regional development responsibilities for Ontario and Quebec. This new, dynamic division of the Government will be responsible for regional economic development in Ontario and Quebec. Will that not give an advantage to central Canada? Will it not have the automatic advantage of putting all these government programs and Departments at their disposal for industrial and economic development?
Will the Western Diversification Office play a co-ordinating role in light of the absolute failure of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion in terms of co-ordination? The Departments of Agriculture, Fisheries, and Mining simply continued programs while ignoring the programs of DREE.
We in the West need an office that will play an advocacy role and will ensure that an issue like the airbus contract will be carefully considered in order to ensure that anything that is done with Air Canada will benefit western Canada. That is what is required.
I realize that my time has expired. My colleagues will have much more to say about this subject. We recognize that there is potential for the Western Diversification Office. It could play a significant role, but it lacks capital and it lacks a mandate.
As Mr. Bulloch of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business calls it, it is a black box. We do not know what it does or what are its terms of reference. That must be changed.

Mr. Speaker, I want to raise a question with my distinguished House Leader because I do not want him to be unaware of the fact that many parts of central Canada also suffer from serious economic problems.
My own constituency has a 9 per cent unemployment rate, and parts of northern Ontario have an unemployment rate well above 10 per cent. One must also recognize that there is a tremendous poverty problem within Toronto, as there is in other cities like Edmonton, Vancouver, and Halifax.
Will he indicate the alternatives we are considering for the country after the next election and outline an approach that does not discriminate against the West nor attempt to follow the traditional political rhetoric of blaming central Canada for problems which exist? After all, it is the Conservative Government, not central Canada, that is responsible for the problems the country faces.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend, the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon), is absolutely correct. In examining the economic hardship facing people in the country today, we have been looking at what is happening in western Canada. In the last few days we have been examining the appalling situation that continues to exist in Atlantic Canada.
As the Member so aptly points out, central Canada is also experiencing severe problems, even in the largest cities. When one considers that the largest city in Canada has the distinction of having one of the largest food banks, I think it tells the tale.
There is an obvious solution. It is to have a new Government. A New Democratic Party Government would set itself apart from the others by a simple distinction. At the top of the list of its priorities, the goal it would set out to achieve as one of the wealthiest countries in the world would be full employment and strategies to accomplish that goal.
One of the first steps should be not only to have a goal of full employment; we should set targets for the lowering of inflation and interest rates. We set targets in a whole range of areas. Why not set a target to lower unemployment not only across Canada but in the regions of the country which the Tories have essentially abandoned? They have abandoned the North, the West, the East, and whole regions of central Canada. Once we start setting a goal of full employment and putting in place strategies to accomplish that goal, once we start setting targets to reduce unemployment, we will be able to make real inroads into reducing the number of jobless and getting economic development back on track where it belongs.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the politically motivated diatribe of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), and I must confess that over the course of his 20-minute speech I had to smile. As a western Canadian I remember full well that his Party was the Party which supported a federal Government

April 29, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
that for years, if not decades, excluded western Canada from its fair share of federal government programs.
In 1984 the Canadian voters in western Canada got the groom by reducing the western representation in the Liberal Party, but we did not get the bride. We reduced her effect, but we will get her in 1988 or 1989.
What we are hearing today is this born again interest in western Canada of the New Democratic Party, the Party that supported the Liberal Party of Canada. The Hon. Member talked about percentages in his speech. He said that British Columbia, having 10 per cent of Canada's population, was receiving 10 per cent or less of some federal government programs, not quite a proportionate share, in some cases.
I understand his argument, but is he suggesting that the sword cut both ways? The Government initiated $1 billion in reforestation funding, of which 30 per cent goes to British Columbia. Should that 30 per cent be reduced to 10 per cent? B.C. sends 30 per cent of unsolicited proposals to the Department of Supply and Services. Should that be reduced to 10 per cent, as well? How about the world's largest ice-breaker commissioned by the Government, $500 million worth? Should we build 10 per cent of that in British Columbia?
What about Phase II of the Salmonid Enhancement Program of $200 million? Should British Columbia only get 10 per cent of that? Is that what the Hon. Member wants, or is he just being selective with his figures? Is he suggesting that British Columbia be restricted to 10 per cent of all federal government programs, that all federal government funding be proportioned according to population, or is he simply having fun with figures this afternoon?

Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to hear the Hon. Member refer to the forest industry. I would think he would be embarrassed to refer to the forest industry, because his Government promised the people of British Columbia, indeed the people of Canada, that if elected it would put in place a full ministry of forests. The Tories failed to do that. Once again, another lie to the people of Canada. They broke another promise because they quite clearly said this was a priority. They are four years into office and we still have not seen this promise delivered. Again I say, another broken promise or even a lie.
Where is the Polar 8? We have heard some announcements, but the action is not there. The Hon. Member asks if British Columbia or the West should have its fair share? Not only should the west have its fair share but, for the next number of years-perhaps even for a two-year or three-year period- could we not have a program called economic affirmative action? Every Canadian understands that the West has been short-changed right from the very beginning. For the next few years, let us have not only a fair share but perhaps even a little more to allow, for instance, the manufacturing sector to be buoyed up. The printers in British Columbia came to Ottawa the other day asking for a fair share.
We are talking about regional industrial support and encouragement. Under the trade deal with the United States that will be impossible. That is what the Hon. Member is suggesting. He advocates, on the one hand, a free trade deal with the United States knowing full well that the minute it is signed regional development programs to support the West will be pulled right away. In other words, he wants to impoverish westerners and discriminate against western Canadians in terms of economic development.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the House Leader of the New Democratic Party in this debate. As a Member of Parliament from the far eastern part of Canada, I want to put on the record that Atlantic Canadian New Democrats also support regional development in western Canada. I know the Deputy House Leader spoke out Wednesday against people from Ontario who supported regional development in Atlantic Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
speechtext: That's nonsense.

I know the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) attacked the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar) for supporting regional development in Atlantic Canada, but I want to put on record that I support regional development in western Canada as well.
Would the Hon. Member care to comment on the attitude the Government seems to have about the fact that only people from eastern Canada can talk about eastern regional development and only people from western Canada can talk about western regional development?

Mr. Speaker, we have heard comments in this House that only can be called regional racism. It was a very sad day when a leader for the government benches felt it was appropriate that debate on an issue of particular interest to Atlantic Canada, be restricted to only Members from Atlantic Canada. I think it should be made clear that those who represent the New Democratic Party represent all Canadians. We represent northerners, easterners, westerners, and people from central Canada. I do not apologize for that. I do not apologize for being part of a Party which cares about Canadians no matter where they live.
I realize the Conservatives have regional interests, that they come from a particular region and do not care about another particular region, but I am proud to be part of a Party that puts Canadians first no matter where they happen to live.
